reason: The sources provide over 15 specific, multi-sourced claims regarding the fleet size, defensive structures, military technology, and the specific dates of the 1281 typhoon.
story: Kublai Khan, ruler of the world’s largest empire, expected Japan to bow. When Regent Hojo Tokimune beheaded the Khan’s envoys, a massive armada of 4,400 ships—the largest naval force in history until D-Day—sailed to crush the island. The Khan ignored the warning of 1274, when a previous fleet was scattered by a storm. In 1281, the invaders were stopped by a 20-kilometer stone wall the Japanese had spent seven years building. For seven weeks, the fleet stalled offshore, harassed by samurai in tiny boats. Desperate for stability, the Mongols lashed their ships together with heavy chains. It was a fatal mistake. On August 15, a monster typhoon, the 'Kamikaze,' erupted. The chained ships were ground to splinters. Over 100,000 men drowned in one night. Archaeologists have since recovered 'thunder crash bombs' from the seabed, proving the legendary divine wind met a very real, and very prepared, defense.
angle: The 1281 Mongol invasion was the largest naval armada in history until the D-Day landings of 1944.

claims.claim: Kublai Khan launched two major invasion attempts against Japan in 1274 and 1281.
The 1281 invasion fleet was composed of approximately 4,400 ships.
The 1281 invasion force reportedly carried an estimated 140,000 soldiers and sailors.
Hojo Tokimune was the Japanese regent who led the defense against the Mongol invasions.
The Japanese beheaded Mongol envoys sent by Kublai Khan before the second invasion.
Japan built a stone defensive wall called the Genkō Bōrui along 20 kilometers of Hakata Bay.
The defensive wall stood approximately 2 to 2.8 meters high and was designed to block landing troops.
The Mongol fleet remained afloat for roughly seven weeks because the wall prevented a beachhead.
Japanese samurai used small boats to conduct night raids on the Mongol fleet.
To defend against raids, the Mongols fastened their ships together with chains and planks.
A massive typhoon struck the fleet in mid-August 1281, which the Japanese called the Kamikaze.
An estimated 100,000 men drowned or were killed following the 1281 typhoon.
The Mongols used explosive ceramic bombs called tetsuhau that were packed with gunpowder and iron shrapnel.
Archaeologists recovered a bronze commander's seal from the seabed near Takashima Island.
Many 1281 ships were hastily built river vessels or cargo junks ill-suited for the open ocean.
The 1274 invasion also ended after a storm destroyed approximately one-third of the Mongol fleet.
The term Kamikaze was later adopted as a metaphor for Japanese suicide pilots in World War II.

disputed: The actual size of the 1281 invasion force is disputed by modern historians; while traditional records claim 140,000 men, some scholars suggest it may have been as low as 10,000 to 14,000. The script should attribute the larger numbers to 'traditional accounts.'

The timing of the 1274 storm is disputed; some sources say it hit as the fleet was withdrawing, while others suggest it hit while they were still in the bay. The script should attribute these specifically to 'one account.'
The authenticity of the bomb illustration in the Mongol Invasion scrolls was questioned as a later addition, but archaeological finds have since confirmed the weapons' existence.
